other_side: NLW's lead is that a new discipline is forming above prompts, context, harnesses and loops — graph engineering, the design of agentic organisations — and that thinking in multi-agent terms is becoming a general work primitive. Zitron's most recent piece treats that whole ladder of new disciplines as narrative rather than demand. His argument is that the money says otherwise: bank analysts now put 70% or more of Microsoft's, Google's and Amazon's AI revenue at OpenAI and Anthropic's own compute spend, so the buildout rests on two loss-making labs rather than on anyone actually getting paid work done. He quotes Apollo's Torsten Slok asking whether ROI will show up for end customers fast enough, and answers "probably not". He also argues the productivity claims are socially coerced — that saying AI is not transforming your job carries professional consequences — and that the real benefit is "much, much less than the boosters will promise".
truth_beneath: Both men orbit one variable: whether orchestrating agents produces work someone will pay for. They agree on more than the tone suggests — that prompt-level skills are near-exhausted, that most corporate AI training is theatre, and that the labs' spending is extraordinary. The empirical question is whether multi-agent systems deliver output an organisation would buy at cost; the observable that settles it is per-seat AI software revenue net of the labs' own compute bills — Microsoft 365 Copilot's disclosed revenue against its claimed thirty million seats is the cleanest test available. The residue is worldview: whether a new engineering discipline signals real capability or a bubble generating vocabulary. Whittemore is vindicated if graph-shaped systems produce durable, sold output; Zitron if the discipline matures while the revenue never arrives. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is that both think the leverage has moved past prompting. Watch whether any vendor discloses agent-product revenue separately from compute.
